difficultyRationale: Targets a widely held misconception the issue explicitly calls out, requiring the distinction between a wiring mechanism and a structural dependency-direction property.
prompt: A team says: 'We use Spring, and Spring does dependency injection, so our code follows the Dependency Inversion Principle.' What is the most accurate assessment of that claim?
explanation: Dependency Injection is a wiring mechanism — something decides what to pass in, and does the passing from outside the object. Dependency Inversion is about which direction the resulting source-code dependency points: whether the high-level module depends on an abstraction it defines, with low-level details depending on that abstraction instead of the other way around. A DI framework can wire concrete-to-concrete dependencies just as easily as abstraction-based ones, so using one is neither proof nor disproof of DIP.

options.text: The claim is accurate, because `@Autowired` by design only resolves dependencies declared through an interface type — never through a field, constructor parameter, or setter parameter typed to a concrete class — so every single injection point that Spring's container touches anywhere in the application is automatically restricted to depending on an abstraction, which is exactly what Dependency Inversion requires.
options.explanation: `@Autowired` works just as well on a field or constructor parameter typed to a concrete class as on one typed to an interface; Spring does not require or enforce an abstraction boundary, so it cannot be relied on to guarantee DIP by itself.

options.text: The claim is false, because Dependency Inversion only applies to languages without a dependency injection framework, like plain C.
options.explanation: DIP is a design principle about the direction of source-code dependencies between modules and is language- and framework-agnostic; it applies equally to code with or without a DI framework, so framework availability isn't what makes the claim right or wrong.

options.text: It conflates a mechanism with a design property: Spring's container can inject any type it's configured with, including a concrete low-level class, so using Spring only guarantees that dependencies arrive from outside the object — it says nothing about whether high-level code depends on an abstraction it owns rather than on a concrete implementation detail.
options.explanation: Correct. The injection mechanism and the direction of the resulting dependency are separate questions; a framework answers the first and is silent on the second.

options.text: The claim is accurate, because `ApplicationContext` is itself an abstraction, so any object it manages automatically depends on an abstraction.
options.explanation: The managed object's own dependencies — what it directly references in its own fields and method signatures — are what DIP judges, not the fact that some external container happens to manage its lifecycle; a bean can still hold a direct reference to a concrete class regardless of who constructs or wires it.

references.title: Martin Fowler — Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection Pattern
